title: What Consumer Centricity Means Today at the Estée Lauder Cos. | United States
text:
Inside the Estée Lauder Cos.' multifaceted approach to keeping with the times, from retail expansions to beauty product virality to AI and more.
Estée Lauder stopped by the Macy's in Herald Square unannounced to see a place setting she designed for a store promotion on September 13, 1989 in New York...
Article title: 'Estee Lauder's CampaignThe story goes that Estée Lauder, then a scrappy founder determined to get her namesake brand into Galeries Lafayette, spilled her Youth Dew fragrance on the department store’s floor, knowing customers would ask to buy it — and that the French retailer would subsequently relent. — albeit at a significantly greater scale, informing the action plans of more than 20 portfolio brands whose combined businesses reached $15 billion in fiscal year 2026.
Victoria Beckham Has Invested More Than $3 Million Into Harper Beckham's Upcoming Skin Care Line “Historically, Estée Lauder has been an amazing company when it comes to delivering the best high-touch experience through counters,” said Aude Gandon, executive vice president, global chief digital and marketing officer at the group.
“Now, it’s basically about delivering that experience everywhere, wherever the consumer is. ” The company is walking the walk, employing myriad strategies to stay current and anticipate consumer needs in an increasingly fast-moving market.
“The world has shifted quite dramatically,” said Amber English, president, digital and online, the Americas, and global Amazon lead at the Estée Lauder Cos. “What we’ve gotten really clear about in the last three to four years is each channel has to play a really important role for consumers…we think about it as, how do we meet the consumer where they are in their journey and service them in the destination they want to be at.
”launched at Sephora for the first time in its 41-year history, expanding the brand’s retail footprint beyond its owned channels, department stores and Ulta Beauty, where it debuted in 2017. In 2024, the Estée Lauder Cos. forayed onto Amazon for the first time with a Clinique storefront, followed by a rollout of storefronts for brands including The Ordinary, Aveda, Bumble & bumble and more.
Meanwhile in 2023, the company seized the opportunity to launch on TikTok Shop with select brands shortly after the platform’s Stateside debut, and has since continued to innovate there through live-selling and cutting-edge creator partnerships. More recently, Estée Lauder Cos. announced a strategic partnership with commerce platform Shopify last fall which will unify omnichannel commerce experiences across the group’s portfolio, thus enabling greater speed and performance.
Tom Ford and Lab Series were the first brands to migrate to Shopify, while MAC most recently transitioned this summer. From virtual try-on to AI-powered experiences the Estée Lauder Cos. is deploying technology across its brands to maximize its relationship with shoppers.
“To be able to take advantage of technology to transform a company, you have to have a solid foundation,” said Brian Franz, chief technology and transformation officer, adding that all of the company’s major brands will be on Shopify — both online and in freestanding stores — by the end of its fiscal 2027. “Being high-touch is one of the things Estée Lauder has just been good at from its inception — from the days of Estée Lauder herself,” said Franz.
“Creating the underlying tech foundation to have this frictionless shopping experience, that’s a really big move forward. ” The partnership also marks a new frontier for Shopify, being the first time the all-in-one commerce platform has worked with a company of Lauder’s scale.
“We’re used to working with founders, and what’s neat about Stéphane is that he acts like a founder,” said Harley Finkelstein, president of Shopify. “There are still companies and leaders out there who think is either one or the other — you’re either online or offline, or you have channel conflict. That’s not how the Lauder team sees it.
They believe that the future of retail, like we do, is wherever customers are — and that’s on- and offline, that’s in agentic commerce, and that’s in places like social media. ” On Amazon, where the company’s successes so far include selling more than 100,000 and 20,000 monthly units respectively of The Ordinary’s Glycolic Acid 7% Exfoliating Toner and Clinique’s Almost Lipstick in Black Honey, Estée Lauder is similarly staying nimble.
“Lauder understands that beauty is a long-term relationship between a brand and its customers, rather than a transaction,” said Wendy Franks, general manager of health and beauty at Amazon U.S. “Together, we have created dedicated Premium Beauty storefronts for ELC where each brand tells its own story, and customers benefit from AI-assisted guidance and authentic reviews so they can shop with confidence.
“For Amazon, this collaboration is significant because it gives our customers access to well-loved brands and the ability to build a complete routine across skin care, makeup, and hair care — whether they are loyal to a brand they have trusted for years or discovering it for the first time — all with the convenience they expect from Amazon. ” More broadly, Lauder is taking an iterative approach to how it harnesses AI to leverage its massive database for actionable insights.
“Data without AI is just a historical sequence of events that have happened… AI without data can’t perform because you just have a hollow architecture without anything to actually harness it for,” said Rakesh Srinivasan, senior vice president of data, analytics and AI at the company. “When data and AI work together — clean, robust data with the appropriate models — is when you really generate value.
” For example, the company has a tool called Formula Navigator which “looks at all the historical data that we have and helps formulators make better decisions when it comes to the types of ingredients to use; if there’s any compliance issues with ingredients, all of these things… essentially helps cut down cycles that would not lead to a lot of value,” said Srinivasan. Lauder also has established a “Never Out of Stock” list featuring more than 50 popular products across the portfolio which, as the title implies, must be kept in stock.
“The importance of those being in stock has such downstream impact to the enterprise that we’ve identified them as the skus that everybody mobilizes around — you can’t do that for 25,000 skus across a portfolio, but you can for about 50 to 100,” English said. Of course, there are circumstances, like social media virality, that the company can’t necessarily plan for that can result in a product going out of stock.
But virality is also a key growth engine for the company.
“The operator in all of us wants to reverse-engineer virality and make everything go viral, but we’ve learned that something that might work really amazing on Clinique may not work on a fragrance brand or a makeup brand or another skin care brand,” said English. Added Gandon: “We keep saying things are moving faster and faster and it’s true; in terms of the way consumers discover brands, the way they make choices, the way they buy — the whole funnel has collapsed completely.
You can discover a brand on TikTok, or on Instagram, and then you basically can buy it in a matter of a few seconds. — there’s always been the trend of what is the new ingredient, what is the new makeup look and so, it’s just heightened because of the new media ecosystem we have,” she said. The company has significantly evolved its operating model to meet this brave new world where it’s at — critically, at the right speed.
“We’re all here to serve the consumer,” said Srinivasan. “At the end of the day, there are times when you can innovate too fast and actually hurt the consumer experience because it’s creating a less-than-optimal consumer experience. ” From virtual try-on to AI-powered experiences the Estée Lauder Cos. is deploying technology across its brands to maximize its relationship with shoppers.
“People have found that when they describe what they like and love in a scent, they kind of pick something different than maybe the most popular scents that Jo Malone sells,” said Franz, adding, “We’re finding more innovative ways to utilize AI in online experiences. ”that help customers ascertain the right products for themselves and shop in more engaging ways, which join existing efforts including in-store and online shade-matching technologies and skin and hair diagnostic tools.
“AI is one of the big enablers of our strategy — building our brand, getting to our consumers, really delivering experiences,” said Franz. “Things fail when it feels like a silo and something separate than like what everybody does every day. The whole executive team works really collaboratively along all these areas. ” The same holds true for IRL experiences as much as digital mastery.
“Lauder has been part of Nordstrom’s beauty business for decades, and that longevity matters,” said Rachel Eichen, vice president and divisional merchandise manager of beauty at Nordstrom. “We’re both family businesses, and we share a deep passion for our customers and our people, and that comes through in the work we do together.
” Earlier this year, Jo Malone London transformed Center Stage, the rotating pop-up space on the main floor of Nordstrom’s New York flagship, into an immersive vegetable garden in celebration of its Brit Veggies Collection, for example.
“The installation brought a playful and unexpected experience that was both visually impactful and immersive to our customers, that felt distinctly Nordstrom and distinctly Jo Malone. Beyond these types of standout moments, we value Lauder’s consistent investment in training our beauty advisers and staying engaged at the counter,” said Eichen.
“The mix of exciting product launches, immersive and experiential storytelling, and everyday consistency in delivering a high standard of expertise and service is what makes our partnership work. ” “If you think about some of our offline experiences, those are immersive; they are beautiful; you can touch and feel — there’s samples, testers; it all plays a role,” said English, adding that there are just as many ways to surprise and delight online, as well.
“We did a Super Brand Day on TikTok Shop with Clinique and what we saw across the entire Honey franchise was remarkable. Amazon search went up within 14 hours. Ulta searches went up, and so we’ve been able to map that as consumers are seeing things on different platforms, all boats rise and consumers are picking which channel they want to convert on, so it’s important that you…understand the interconnectivity of all of those different efforts.
” While the future is never certain, the balance between experimentation and authenticity at Estée Lauder — and among its consumers — is a constant.
“What is at the core of Estée Lauder brands is that we do a lot of deep work to understand who our brands are, and what they stand for,” said English. “You don’t lose touch with the soul of your brand — you evolve with it; how you show up or innovate might differ, but your soul doesn’t change.
” Added Franz: “It goes back to what Stéphane set in the core strategy of speed and agility, and having the consumer at the heart of everything we’re doing. That has, from my standpoint, permeated the organization, and that’s what everybody talks about right now.
“We’re still brand builders, but at the same time,” he said, “we’re building brands for consumers, and we have to be where the consumer is. ”WWD and Women's Wear Daily are part of PMX Global, LLC, a subsidiary of Penske Media Corporation. © 2026 Fairchild Publishing, LLC. All rights reserved.
